doc.title: Ruthie Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 28, 2023

title: Poetry, Maya Angelou and writing poems for cousins
summary: She treats lyrics like poetry, started writing poems young, loved Black poets, and wrote poems for friends for money.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Do you read through your lyrics when they’re in progress as if they’re a poem?

Yeah. I do. I do. Melodically, melody is important to me. Groove is even, right up there with melody, but it’s about the words, the lyrics and I started out writing poetry as a © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

young person. Some of my favorite poets were Dr. Maya Angelou and Gwendolyn Brooks, Nikki Giovanni, which I actually got a chance to talk to and see. These were some of my favorites, you know black poetresses. That was huge for me, growing up in the small town, being this little black girl in the middle of Texas. I wanted to read something that I could relate to, something that was written that said, basically told me — gave me an idea that someone else out there like me, and Maya Angelou was huge in my life during that period. I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings — that was huge. It blew the doors off of my feeling like I’m the only one out here who really loves the way of poetry and what poetry does for you, and how it moves you. And even in high school one of the ways I would actually make a little extra money, I wrote poems for my friends. Basically I had a lot of cousins. I had 22 cousins growing up. A lot of us lived all around each other. And you know my cousin Sherry — she had a new boyfriend, she wanted a new poem written about them so I’d just do that and then charge them a little bit of money for it. So that’s how I started out, writing poems myself. So yeah reading lyrics, very much like poetry for me. It has a lot to do with the songs I pick too, to record.
